div.p: Let us speak of the art of poetry itself and of its species, what capacity each possesses, and how plots must be constructed if the poetic composition is to be well made, and further from how many and what sort of parts it consists, and likewise of all other matters belonging to the same inquiry, beginning in the natural order first from first principles.
Epic poetry, then, and the composition of tragedy, and also comedy and dithyrambic poetry, and the greater part of flute-playing and lyre-playing, are all, viewed as a whole, forms of imitation.
They differ from one another in three respects: either by imitating in different media, or by imitating different objects, or by imitating in a different manner and not in the same way.

For just as some people imitate many things by producing likenesses with colors and figures (some through art, others through habit), and others through the voice, so too in the arts mentioned above, all produce their imitation in rhythm, language, and melody, using these either separately or combined.
For instance, flute-playing and lyre-playing use melody and rhythm alone, and any other arts that happen to have a similar capacity, such as the art of panpipes;
the art of dancers imitates by rhythm itself without melody (for they too imitate characters, emotions, and actions through rhythmic figures);

while the art epic poetry that uses bare language alone and the one that uses meters—and in the latter case whether mixing different meters with one another or using a single kind of meter—happen to be nameless up to the present time.
For we would have no common name to give to the mimes of Sophron and Xenarchus and the Socratic dialogues,
nor if someone were to make his imitation in trimeters or elegiacs or any other such meters.

People, however, attaching the word "making" to the meter, call some elegiac-makers and others epic-makers, naming them not as poets in virtue of imitation, but indiscriminately according to their meter.

Indeed, even if someone publishes a medical or scientific treatise in meter, they are accustomed to call him a poet; yet Homer and Empedocles have nothing in common except their meter, so that it is right to call the former a poet, but the latter a natural philosopher rather than a poet.

Likewise, even if someone produces his imitation by mixing all the meters together, just as Chaeremon composed his Centaur, a mixed rhapsody in all meters, he too must be called a poet. Let these distinctions, then, be drawn in this way.

There are certain arts that use all the means mentioned—I mean rhythm, song, and meter—such as dithyrambic poetry, the composition of nomes, tragedy, and comedy; they differ, however, in that the former use all of them simultaneously, while the latter use them in separate parts.
These, then, are what I call the differences of the arts with respect to the media in which they produce their imitation.

Since those who imitate imitate people in action, and these must necessarily be either admirable or inferior (for character almost always follows these two categories alone, since everyone differs in character by vice and virtue), they must imitate people either better than we are, or worse, or like ourselves, just as painters do.
For Polygnotus portrayed better people, Pauson worse, and Dionysius people like ourselves.
It is clear that each of the imitations we have mentioned will also have these differences, and will be distinct by imitating different objects in this manner.
For in dancing, flute-playing, and lyre-playing these dissimilarities can arise,

and also in prose and unaccompanied verse: for example, Homer represents better people, Cleophon people like ourselves, while Hegemon of Thasos, the first to compose parodies, and Nicochares, author of the Deiliad, represent worse people.
So too in dithyrambs and nomes: one could imitate just as Timotheus and Philoxenus imitated the Cyclopes.
It is in this very difference that tragedy stands apart from comedy: comedy aims to imitate people worse, and tragedy people better, than those of the present day.
There is still a third difference among these, namely the manner in which one may imitate each of these objects.

For it is possible to imitate the same objects in the same media sometimes by narrating—either becoming someone else, as Homer does, or remaining the same person without changing—or by representing all the characters as acting and engaging in activity.
Imitation, then, consists in these three differences, as we said at the beginning: the media, the objects, and the manner.

Thus in one respect Sophocles would be the same kind of imitator as Homer, since both imitate admirable people, and in another respect the same as Aristophanes, since both imitate people acting and doing. Hence some say that these works are called dramas, because they imitate people doing things.

That is why the Dorians lay claim to both tragedy and comedy—comedy is claimed by the Megarians, both those here on the ground that it arose during their democracy, and those in Sicily, since the poet Epicharmus came from there and was much earlier than Chionides and Magnes; and tragedy is claimed by some of the Peloponnesians—using the names as evidence.

For they say that they themselves call outlying villages komai, whereas the Athenians call them demes, assuming that comedians were named not from reveling (komazein) but from wandering through the villages when dishonored and driven out of the city; and that they themselves call doing dran, whereas the Athenians call it prattein.
So much, then, for the differences of imitation, how many and what they are.
In general, two causes seem to have given birth to the art of poetry, and both of them are natural.

For imitating is innate in human beings from childhood, and they differ from the other animals in that man is the most imitative of creatures and acquires his first pieces of knowledge through imitation; and everyone takes pleasure in imitations.

A sign of this is what happens in practice: things that we look upon with pain in themselves, we delight in viewing when they are most accurately rendered in images, such as the forms of the vilest beasts and of corpses.
The reason for this too is that learning is most pleasant not only to philosophers but likewise to everyone else, though they share in it only to a small extent.
For people take pleasure in looking at images because as they view them they learn and infer what each thing is, for instance, "that man is so-and-so."
For if one happens not to have seen the subject before, the image will not produce its pleasure as an imitation, but because of the craftsmanship, or the color, or some other such cause.

Since imitating is natural to us, as are melody and rhythm (for it is obvious that meters are parts of rhythms), from the beginning those who were most naturally gifted for them gradually advanced them and generated poetry out of improvisations.

Poetry then split apart according to the poets' own characters: the more dignified imitated noble actions and those of noble people, while the more trivial imitated those of inferior people, composing invectives at first, just as the others composed hymns and encomia.
Of the poets before Homer we cannot name any such poem, though it is likely that there were many;

beginning from Homer, however, we can, such as his Margites and works of that kind. In these, as was fitting, the iambic meter also came in—which is why it is now called iambic, because in this meter they lampooned (iambizein) one another.
And of the ancients, some became poets of heroic verse and others of iambics.

Just as Homer was the supreme poet in serious matters (for he alone not only composed well, but also made dramatic imitations), so too he was the first to outline the form of comedy, dramatizing not invective but the laughable. For the Margites stands in the same relation to comedies as the Iliad and the Odyssey stand to tragedies.

Once tragedy and comedy had come to light, those who were drawn to each kind of poetry according to their own nature became comic poets instead of iambic poets, and tragic poets instead of epic poets, because these forms were grander and more esteemed than the earlier ones. Whether or not tragedy is now sufficiently developed in its constituent forms, judged both in itself and in relation to audiences, is another question.

Having come into being, then, from an improvisational beginning—both tragedy itself and comedy, the one from the leaders of the dithyramb, the other from the leaders of the phallic songs that still remain customary in many cities—tragedy gradually grew as poets developed each element of it that came to light;
and after undergoing many changes, tragedy stopped changing once it had attained its own proper nature.

Aeschylus was the first to raise the number of actors from one to two, reduced the part of the chorus, and made spoken dialogue take the leading role; Sophocles introduced three actors and scene-painting.
Further, as to magnitude: from small plots and laughable diction, because it developed out of a satyr-like form, it acquired dignity only late, and its meter changed from tetrameter to iambic.

At first they used the tetrameter because the poetry was satyr-like and more suited to dancing; but when spoken dialogue came in, nature herself discovered the appropriate meter, for the iambic is the most conversational of meters. A sign of this is that
we speak iambics very often in our conversation with one another, whereas we rarely speak hexameters, and only when we depart from conversational rhythm.

Further, there was the number of episodes. And as for all the other ways in which each part is said to have been embellished, Missing text? λέγεται. περὶ μὲν οὖν τούτω τοσαῦτα ἔστω let us take them as already stated;
for it would perhaps be a great task to go through them one by one.
Comedy, as we said, is an imitation of inferior people—not, however, with respect to every kind of vice, but insofar as the laughable is a subdivision of the ugly.
For the laughable is a sort of flaw and ugliness that is painless and not destructive, just as, for an immediate example, the comic mask is ugly and distorted without pain.

Now the transformations of tragedy and the men who brought them about have not escaped notice, whereas comedy escaped notice because it was not taken seriously at first; indeed, it was only late that the archon granted a chorus of comic performers, who previously were volunteers.
It is only after comedy already had certain definite forms that its so-called poets are remembered. Who introduced masks or prologues or numbers of actors and all such things is unknown.
The making of plots Epicharmus and Phormis originally came from Sicily;
among the Athenians, Crates was the first to abandon the iambic form and begin composing generalized stories and plots.
Epic poetry, then, agrees with tragedy insofar as it is an imitation of admirable people in language with meter; they differ, however, in that epic has a single meter and is narrative.

They also differ in length: tragedy tries as far as possible to stay within a single revolution of the sun or to exceed it only slightly, whereas epic is unlimited in time, and differs in this respect—
although at first they did this in tragedies in the same way as in epics.
As for their constituent parts, some are the same, while others are peculiar to tragedy.
Consequently, whoever knows about good and bad tragedy also knows about epic; for all the elements that epic possesses belong to tragedy, whereas not all that belong to tragedy are found in epic.
We shall speak later about imitation in hexameters and about comedy; let us now speak of tragedy, taking up the definition of its essence that results from what has been said.

Tragedy, then, is an imitation of an action that is admirable, complete, and possesses magnitude; in language made pleasurable, each of its species separately in different parts; performed by actors, not through narration; effecting through pity and fear the purification of such emotions.
By "pleasurable language" I mean language that has rhythm and melody and song;
and by "the species separately," that some parts are carried out through meters alone and others again through song.

Since they produce the imitation by acting, in the first place the ordering of spectacle must necessarily be a part of tragedy; and then song-making and diction, for it is in these media that they produce the imitation.
By "diction" I mean the very composition of the verses, and by "song-making" that whose meaning is entirely evident.

Since it is an imitation of an action, and an action is performed by certain agents, who must necessarily have certain qualities of character and thought (for it is because of these that we say actions too are of a certain quality, there are naturally two causes of actions, thought and character and in accordance with these everyone either succeeds or fails),

the plot is the imitation of the action—for by "plot" I mean here the structuring of the events—while "character" is that in virtue of which we say that the agents are of a certain quality, and "thought" is everything in which speakers demonstrate something or also state a general maxim.
Necessarily, then, there are six parts of every tragedy, according to which tragedy has its particular quality; these are plot, character, diction, thought, spectacle, and song-making.
For two parts are the media in which they imitate, one is the manner in which they imitate, and three are the objects that they imitate; and beyond these there is nothing.
Not a few of the poets, so to speak, have used these forms; for every tragedy has spectacle, character, plot, diction, song, and thought alike.

The most important of these is the structuring of the events. For tragedy is an imitation not of human beings, but of action and of life and happiness and unhappiness reside in action, and the end is a certain kind of action, not a quality; people are of a certain quality according to their characters, but according to their actions they are happy or the opposite.

Therefore they do not act in order to imitate characters, but they include characters for the sake of the actions; so that the events and the plot are the end of tragedy, and the end is the most important thing of all.
Furthermore, without action there could not be a tragedy, whereas without character there could.

For the tragedies of most of the recent poets are devoid of character, and in general many poets are like that, just as among painters Zeuxis stands in relation to Polygnotus: Polygnotus is a good painter of character, whereas the painting of Zeuxis has no character at all.

Again, if someone strings together speeches expressive of character that are well crafted in diction and thought, he will not achieve what is the proper function of tragedy; far more will a tragedy that is inferior in these respects, yet possesses a plot and structuring of events.
In addition to this, the most powerful means by which tragedy moves the soul are parts of the plot, namely reversals and recognitions.
A further sign is that beginners in poetry are able to achieve precision in diction and character sooner than in structuring events, as was the case with nearly all the earliest poets.
The plot, then, is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of tragedy, while character holds second place.
(It is much the same in painting: if someone were to smear on the most beautiful colors at random, it would not give as much pleasure as a portrait sketched in outline.)
Tragedy is an imitation of an action, and principally for the sake of the action, an imitation of the agents.
Third is thought: this is the ability to say what is inherent in a situation and appropriate to it, which in speeches is the function of politics and rhetoric.
For the older poets made their characters speak like statesmen, whereas those of today make them speak like rhetoricians.

Character is the sort of thing that reveals moral choice, of whatever kind it is in situations where it is not obvious what someone chooses or avoids; hence there is no character in speeches in which there is nothing at all that the speaker chooses or avoids.
Thought is found where speakers demonstrate that something is or is not the case, or make some universal statement.
Fourth among the verbal elements is diction; and by diction, as was said before, I mean expression through the choice of words, which has the same force both in verse and in prose.
Of the remaining parts, song-making is the greatest of the embellishments;

while spectacle is emotionally engaging, yet least artistic and least integral to the art of poetry. For the power of tragedy exists even without performance and actors, and moreover the art of the stage-designer is more decisive for the production of visual effects than that of the poets.
Now that these distinctions have been made, let us next discuss what kind of structuring of the events is required, since this is both the first and the most important element of tragedy.
We have laid down that tragedy is an imitation of a complete and whole action possessing a certain magnitude; for a thing can be a whole and yet possess no magnitude.
A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
A beginning is that which does not itself necessarily follow anything else, but after which something else naturally exists or comes to be.
An end, conversely, is that which itself naturally follows something else, either of necessity or for the most part, while nothing else comes after it.
A middle is that which both itself follows something else and is followed by something else.
Well-constructed plots, therefore, must neither begin at some random point nor end at some random point, but must employ the principles just stated.

Furthermore, since a beautiful thing—whether a living creature or any object composed of parts—must not only have those parts arranged in order, but must also possess a magnitude that is not just any random size (for beauty consists in magnitude and order),

consequently neither could a very tiny creature be beautiful (since our view of it is confused, occurring in an almost imperceptible time), nor a very huge one (since our view does not take place all at once, and the unity and wholeness escape the viewers' contemplation)—for instance, if a creature were ten thousand stades long.
Therefore, just as bodies and living creatures must have magnitude, yet one easily taken in at a single view, so too plots must have length, yet one easily held in memory.

As for the limit of length, the one determined by dramatic competitions and sense-perception does not belong to the art; for if a hundred tragedies had to compete, they would compete by the water-clock, as they say used to happen at some other time.

But as for the limit determined by the actual nature of the matter, the greater the plot, so long as it remains clearly intelligible as a whole, the finer it is in respect of magnitude; to give a simple definition, whatever magnitude allows a change from bad fortune to good fortune, or from good fortune to bad fortune, to occur through a sequence of events according to probability or necessity, is a sufficient limit of magnitude.

A plot is not unified, as some suppose, merely if it is about one person. For countless things happen to a single person, some of which form no unity at all; and in the same way a single person performs many actions, out of which no single action arises.
Therefore all those poets seem to err who have composed a Heracleid, a Theseid, or other poems of that sort; they think that because Heracles was one person, his plot ought also to be one.

Homer, however, just as he excels in other respects, seems to have seen this clearly as well, whether by art or by nature. In composing the Odyssey, he did not include everything that ever happened to Odysseus—such as his being wounded on Mount Parnassus or his feigning madness at the muster, neither of which made it necessary or probable that the other should happen—but he constructed the Odyssey around a single action of the sort we mean, and likewise the Iliad.

Accordingly, just as in the other imitative arts a single imitation is of a single object, so too the plot, since it is an imitation of an action, must be of a single and whole action, and the parts of the events must be so structured that if any part is displaced or removed, the whole is disjointed and disturbed. For whatever makes no noticeable difference whether it is present or absent is no real part of the whole.
It is also clear from what has been said that the function of a poet is not to relate what has happened, but what might happen—things that are possible according to probability or necessity.

For the historian and the poet do not differ by speaking in verse or in prose (the work of Herodotus could be put into verse, and it would still be a kind of history no less in verse than without verse); rather, they differ in that the one relates what has happened, while the other relates what might happen.
For this reason poetry is both more philosophical and more serious than history; for poetry speaks rather of universals, whereas history speaks of particulars.

A universal is the sort of thing that a certain kind of person will say or do according to probability or necessity, which is what poetry aims at even while attaching individual names; a particular is what Alcibiades did or what happened to him.

In comedy this has already become clear: having constructed the plot through probabilities, comic poets then assign whatever names they please, and do not compose about a particular individual as the iambic poets do.

In tragedy, however, they cling to historical names. The reason is that what is possible is convincing; now we do not yet believe that what has not happened is possible, whereas what has happened is obviously possible, for it would not have happened if it were impossible.

Nevertheless, even in tragedies there are some in which only one or two of the names are familiar and the rest are invented, and in some none at all, as in Agathon's Antheus; for in this play both the events and the names are invented alike, and it gives no less pleasure.

Consequently one must not seek at all costs to cling to the traditional stories around which tragedies are built. Indeed, it is absurd to insist on this, since even the familiar stories are familiar only to a few, and yet they give pleasure to all.
It is clear from these considerations, then, that a poet must be a maker of plots rather than of verses, inasmuch as he is a poet in virtue of imitation, and what he imitates are actions.

And even if he happens to compose about actual events, he is nonetheless a poet; for nothing prevents some actual events from being such as would probably happen and could possibly happen, and it is in that respect that he is their poet.
Of simple plots and actions, the episodic are the worst. By an episodic plot I mean one in which the sequence of episodes is neither probable nor necessary.

Such plots are composed by bad poets on their own account, and by good poets on account of the actors; for in composing display pieces and stretching the plot beyond its capacity, they are often forced to distort the logical sequence.

Since the imitation is not only of a complete action, but also of fearful and pitiable events, these arise most of all and even more when they happen contrary to expectation yet because of one another.

For the element of wonder will be greater in this way than if they happen spontaneously and by chance, since even among chance occurrences those seem most wondrous that appear to have happened as if by design—for instance, how the statue of Mitys at Argos killed the man responsible for Mitys' death by falling upon him while he was watching a festival; for such events do not seem to occur at random.
Plots of this kind, therefore, are necessarily finer.
Of plots, some are simple and others complex; for the actions of which plots are imitations are straightaway of these two kinds.
By a simple action I mean one whose course is continuous and unified, as defined above, and in which the change of fortune takes place without reversal or recognition;
by a complex action, one in which the change of fortune is accompanied by recognition or reversal or both.

These must arise from the very structure of the plot, so that from what has happened before they follow either by necessity or by probability; for it makes a great difference whether these things happen because of those or merely after those.
Reversal is a change of the actions to their opposite, as has been said, and this too, as we maintain, according to probability or necessity.
For example, in the Oedipus, the messenger came intending to cheer Oedipus and free him from his fear regarding his mother, yet by revealing who he was, he achieved the opposite;
and in the Lynceus, Lynceus was being led away to die while Danaus followed to kill him, yet it turned out from the course of events that Danaus died and Lynceus was saved.
Recognition, as the very name indicates, is a change from ignorance to knowledge, leading either to friendship or to enmity among those marked out for good or bad fortune.
The finest recognition is one that occurs simultaneously with a reversal, such as the one in the Oedipus.
There are indeed other kinds of recognition: for it can occur in relation to inanimate and random objects, as has been said, and one can recognize whether someone has done a thing or not.

But the kind that belongs most to plot and most to action is the one just described; for such a recognition and reversal will evoke either pity or fear (and tragedy is assumed to be an imitation of actions of that sort), since both bad fortune and good fortune will come about in such cases.

Since recognition is recognition of persons, some recognitions are of one person by the other only, when it is already clear who the other is, while sometimes both must recognize each other: for instance, Iphigenia was recognized by Orestes from the sending of the letter, whereas another recognition was needed for him to be recognized by Iphigenia.
These, then, are two parts of the plot, reversal and recognition; a third is suffering. Reversal and recognition have been explained;
suffering is a destructive or painful action, such as deaths in full view, agonies, woundings, and all things of that sort.

The parts of tragedy that must be used as its constituent forms we have stated earlier; quantitatively, the separate sections into which it is divided are these: prologue, episode, exode, and choral part,
the last being divided into parode and stasimon.
These are common to all tragedies, whereas songs from the stage and kommoi are peculiar to some.
A prologue is an entire part of a tragedy preceding the chorus's parode;
an episode is an entire part of a tragedy between complete choral songs;
an exode is an entire part of a tragedy after which there is no choral song.
Of the choral part, a parode is the first complete utterance of a chorus;
a stasimon is a choral song without anapests or trochees;
a kommos is a lament shared by the chorus and the actors on stage.
The parts of tragedy that must be used as constituent forms we stated earlier; quantitatively, the separate sections into which it is divided are these.

What one should aim at and what one should guard against in constructing plots, and from what source the proper effect of tragedy will arise, should be discussed next in sequence after what has just been said.

Since, then, the structure of the finest tragedy must be not simple but complex, and must be imitative of fearful and pitiable events (for this is the distinctive mark of such imitation), it is clear in the first place that decent men must not be shown passing from good fortune to bad fortune, for that is neither fearful nor pitiable, but repulsive;
nor depraved men from bad fortune to good fortune, for that is the most untragic of all, having none of the qualities required, since it is neither morally satisfying nor pitiable nor fearful;

nor again should a thoroughly wicked man fall from good fortune into bad fortune, for such a structure might satisfy moral feeling, yet it would evoke neither pity nor fear—for pity concerns the man who suffers undeservedly, and fear concerns one like ourselves (pity for the undeserving, fear for one like ourselves)—so that the outcome will be neither pitiable nor fearful.

There remains, then, the person intermediate between these. Such is a man who neither excels in virtue and justice nor falls into misfortune through vice and depravity, but through some error—one of those who enjoy great renown and prosperity, such as Oedipus, Thyestes, and illustrious men from families of that kind.

A well-constructed plot, therefore, must necessarily be single rather than double, as some claim, and must change not from bad fortune to good fortune, but on the contrary from good fortune to bad fortune, not through depravity but through a great error on the part of a man such as we have described, or one better rather than worse.

What actually happens is a sign of this: at first the poets recounted any stories that came to hand, whereas nowadays the finest tragedies are composed around a few houses, such as those of Alcmaeon, Oedipus, Orestes, Meleager, Thyestes, Telephus, and any others whose lot it has been either to suffer or to do terrible things.
The finest tragedy according to the art, then, comes from this structure.
Hence those who criticize Euripides make the very same mistake when they fault him for doing this in his tragedies and ending most of them in misfortune. For this, as has been said, is right.

The greatest sign is that on the stage and in competitions such plays appear the most tragic, if they are well executed, and Euripides, even if he does not manage other matters well, nevertheless appears the most tragic of the poets.
Second best is the structure that some call first—the one that has a double construction, like the Odyssey, and ends in opposite ways for the better and worse characters.
It is thought to be first because of the weakness of audiences; for the poets follow along, composing to suit the spectators' wishes.

Yet this is not the pleasure that comes from tragedy, but belongs rather to comedy; for there, those who are the bitterest enemies in the story, such as Orestes and Aegisthus, walk off as friends at the end, and no one is killed by anyone.
Now the fearful and pitiable can arise from spectacle, and they can also arise from the very structure of the events, which is superior and the mark of a better poet.

For the plot should be so constructed that even without seeing it, anyone who hears the events taking place both shudders and feels pity at what happens—just as one would feel on hearing the plot of the Oedipus.
To produce this effect through spectacle is less artistic and requires financial outlay.

Those who use spectacle to produce not the fearful, but merely the monstrous, have nothing in common with tragedy; for one must not seek every kind of pleasure from tragedy, but the pleasure proper to it.
And since the poet must produce the pleasure that comes from pity and fear through imitation, it is clear that this must be built into the events.
Let us grasp, then, what sorts of occurrences appear terrible or pitiable. Necessarily such actions take place between friends, or between enemies, or between people who are neither.
Now if an enemy acts against an enemy, there is nothing pitiable either in doing the deed or in intending it, except for the suffering itself;
nor if they are neutral toward one another.

But when the sufferings occur within close relationships— for instance, when brother kills brother, or son father, or mother son, or son mother, or intends to do so, or commits some other such deed—these are what must be sought.
One cannot undo the traditional stories—I mean, for example, Clytemnestra's being killed by Orestes and Eriphyle by Alcmaeon—
but the poet must invent for himself and use the traditional material well. Let us state more clearly what we mean by "well."
The action may be performed as the older poets represented it, with full knowledge and awareness, just as Euripides represented Medea killing her children.

Or one may perform the terrible deed in ignorance, and afterward recognize the bond of kinship, like Sophocles' Oedipus; in that case the deed lies outside the play, whereas inside the tragedy itself we have examples like the Alcmaeon of Astydamas or Telegonus in the Wounded Odysseus.
Still a third possibility besides these is to be on the point of doing something irreparable in ignorance, and to recognize the truth before doing it.
And besides these there is no other way: one must either act or not act, and either with knowledge or without knowledge.

Of these, to intend to act with full knowledge and then fail to act is the worst: it is repulsive, and not tragic, because it lacks suffering. Accordingly no one composes in this way, except rarely, as Haemon against Creon in the Antigone.
To perform the deed is second worst.
Better is to act in ignorance and to recognize the truth after acting; for there is nothing repulsive in it, and the recognition is startling.

Best of all is the last: I mean, for example, in the Cresphontes Merope is about to kill her son, yet does not kill him, but recognizes him; and in the Iphigenia the sister recognizes her brother; and in the Helle the son, on the point of handing over his mother, recognizes her.

For this reason, as was said long ago, tragedies are not about many families. For in their search, the poets discovered not by art but by chance how to produce this effect in their plots; so they are compelled to have recourse to those houses in which such sufferings have occurred.
Regarding the structuring of the events, then, and what sorts of plots are required, enough has been said.
With regard to character, there are four things to aim at. One, and the first, is that it should be good.
A play will have character if, as was stated, speech or action makes clear some moral choice, whatever it may be, and good character if the choice is good.
Goodness is possible in each class of person: for both a woman can be good and a slave, even though perhaps the former is inferior and the latter is altogether base.
The second thing is appropriateness: a character can be manly, yet it is not appropriate for a woman to be manly or clever in this way.
The third is likeness to life; for this is different from making character good and appropriate in the senses already stated.
The fourth is consistency: for even if the person who provides the subject of the imitation is inconsistent, and such a character is posited, still he must be consistently inconsistent.
An example of unnecessary depravity of character is Menelaus in the Orestes;
of the unseemly and inappropriate, the lament of Odysseus in the Scylla and the speech of Melanippe;
of the inconsistent, Iphigenia at Aulis, for the girl who begs for her life is not at all like the later Iphigenia.

In characterization, just as in the structuring of events, one must always seek either the necessary or the probable, so that it is either necessary or probable that such a person should say or do such things, and either necessary or probable that this should happen after that.
It is clear, then, that the resolutions of plots too must arise from the plot itself, and not by a stage machine as in the Medea, or in the episode of the departure in the Iliad.

Rather, the machine should be used for things outside the drama—either events that happened before it which no human being could know, or events after it which require foretelling and announcement; for we grant to the gods the power to see all things.
There should be nothing irrational in the events; or if there is, it should be outside the tragedy, like the irrationality in Sophocles' Oedipus.

Since tragedy is an imitation of people better than ourselves, poets must imitate good portrait-painters: for they too, while reproducing the individual's distinctive form and making a likeness, paint him handsomer than he is. So too the poet, when imitating people who are irascible or indolent or have other such traits of character, should make them admirable while keeping them such—just as Homer portrayed Achilles as an example of harshness and yet noble.

These points, then, one must observe, and in addition those that concern the sense-perceptions necessarily accompanying the poetic art; for one can often go wrong in these as well. Enough, however, has been said about them in my published writings.
What recognition is has been stated earlier. As for the species of recognition, the first is the least artistic and the one most used out of lack of resource: recognition through tokens.
Of these, some are congenital, such as the spear which the Earth-born bear
or the stars such as Carcinus used in his Thyestes; others are acquired, and of these some are on the body, such as scars, and others external, such as necklaces, or the cradle in the Tyro.
Even these tokens, however, can be used better or worse: for example, Odysseus was recognized by his scar in one way by the nurse and in another way by the swineherds.
Recognitions contrived for the sake of proof, and all such, are less artistic, whereas those arising from a reversal, like the one in the Washing Scene, are better.

Second are recognitions manufactured by the poet, and therefore inartistic. For instance, Orestes in the Iphigenia revealed that he was Orestes: she was recognized through the letter, whereas he himself says what the poet wants, not what the plot demands;
hence this comes close to the fault just mentioned, since he might just as well have brought along some tokens too. Another example is the "voice of the shuttle" in Sophocles' Tereus.

The third kind is through memory, when seeing something awakens a feeling—as in the Cyprians of Dicaeogenes, where the hero wept on seeing the painting, and in the Tale of Alcinous, where Odysseus wept on hearing the lyre-player and remembering the past, and thus they were recognized.

Fourth is recognition from reasoning, as in the Choephori: "Someone like me has come; no one is like me except Orestes; therefore Orestes has come." So too the suggestion of Polyidus the sophist regarding the Iphigenia: he said it was probable that Orestes should reason that his sister had been sacrificed and that it was now his own lot to be sacrificed. And in the Tydeus of Theodectes, the father says that having come to find his son he is himself perishing. And the recognition in the Phineidae: on seeing the place, the women inferred their fate, that it was fated for them to die there, since they had also been exposed there.

There is also a composite kind arising from false reasoning on the part of the audience, as in the Odysseus the False Messenger: that he could string the bow and no one else could is a contrivance of the poet and a premise, and so too if he said he would recognize the bow which he had not seen; but to make the audience assume he would recognize it through that means is a fallacy.

Best of all recognitions is that which arises from the events themselves, the astonishment coming about through probabilities, as in Sophocles' Oedipus and the Iphigenia (for it is natural that she should wish to send a letter). For such recognitions alone dispense with contrived tokens and necklaces.
Second best are those from reasoning.

In constructing plots and working them out in diction, one should set them as vividly as possible before one's eyes; for in this way, seeing them most clearly as if present at the very events, one will discover what is fitting and will least overlook any inconsistencies.

A sign of this is the criticism made against Carcinus: Amphiaraus was coming back out of a temple, which escaped notice if one did not visualize it the spectator, yet on stage the play failed because the audience was annoyed by this.

So far as possible, one should even work out the play with the gestures themselves; for those who are actually in the grip of the emotions are most convincing by virtue of their shared human nature, and one who is agitated expresses agitation and one who is angry expresses anger most truthfully.
Hence the art of poetry belongs to a naturally gifted person or to a madman: the former are adaptable, the latter are carried outside themselves.
Both stories already composed and those one invents oneself should be set out in general outline, and only then expanded into episodes and lengthened.

What I mean by viewing the general outline can be seen in the case of the Iphigenia: a certain maiden was sacrificed and vanished mysteriously from those who sacrificed her, and being settled in another land, where it was the custom to sacrifice strangers to the goddess, she held this priesthood. Some time later it happened that the priestess's brother arrived—the fact that the god gave an oracle for some reason outside the general outline bidding him go there, and the purpose of his journey, lie outside the plot. Arriving and being captured, as he is about to be sacrificed he reveals his identity, whether as Euripides or as Polyidus contrived it, remarking with probability that not only his sister, then, but he too was destined to be sacrificed; and from this comes his rescue.
Only after this should the poet supply the names and develop the episodes.
One must see that the episodes are germane to the plot, such as in the case of Orestes the madness through which he was captured and his rescue through the purification.
Now in dramas the episodes are concise, whereas epic poetry is lengthened by them.

For the story of the Odyssey is not long: a certain man is away from home for many years, closely watched by Poseidon and left alone; meanwhile affairs at home are in such a state that his property is being consumed by suitors and his son is being plotted against; he himself arrives after enduring storms, reveals himself to certain people, attacks, and is himself saved while destroying his enemies.
That is the essential story; everything else is episodes.
Every tragedy has a complication and a resolution: the events outside the play and often some of those inside it form the complication, and the rest forms the resolution.

By "complication" I mean everything from the beginning up to that final part from which the change to good fortune or bad fortune takes place; by "resolution," everything from the beginning of the change to the end.

For example, in the Lynceus of Theodectes, the complication consists of the prior events, the seizure of the child, and then their own seizure; the resolution is everything from the accusation of murder to the end.
There are four species of tragedy (for the same number of constituent parts was mentioned):
the complex, which consists wholly of reversal and recognition;
the tragedy of suffering, such as the Ajaxes and the Ixions;
the tragedy of character, such as the Phthiotides and the Peleus;
and the fourth is the simple (or spectacular), such as the Phorcides, the Prometheus, and all plays set in Hades.

Ideally, then, one should try to include all four, or failing that, the greatest and most of them—especially given the way critics nowadays carp at poets: because there have been good poets in each individual element, they demand that a single poet surpass the distinctive excellence of each.
It is right to call a tragedy different or the same on no basis so much as the plot—that is, when the complication and resolution are the same.
Many poets who construct the complication well handle the resolution badly;
both, however, must be mastered equally.
One must remember what has been said many times and not turn a tragedy into an epic structure—by "epic" I mean having multiple plots—as if someone were to dramatize the entire story of the Iliad.
In epic, because of its length, the parts receive their proper scale, whereas in dramas the result falls far short of expectation.

A sign of this is that all who have composed the Sack of Troy as a whole and not in part like Euripides, or the story of Niobe and not as Aeschylus did, either fail completely or fare badly in competition; indeed, Agathon himself failed in this point alone.
In reversals and in simple actions, however, poets hit their mark wonderfully; for this is both tragic and morally satisfying.
This happens when a clever but wicked man is outwitted, like Sisyphus, and a brave but unjust man is defeated.
And this is also probable, as Agathon says: for it is probable that many things should happen even contrary to probability.
The chorus too should be treated as one of the actors, and be a part of the whole and share in the action—not as in Euripides, but as in Sophocles.

In the remaining poets, the songs sung belong no more to the plot than to any other tragedy; hence they sing interludes, a practice first begun by Agathon. Yet what difference is there between singing interludes and transferring a speech or an entire episode from one play into another?
The other constituent elements have now been discussed; it remains to speak of diction and thought.
Now what concerns thought may be left to our treatise on Rhetoric, for it belongs more properly to that discipline.
Under thought fall all the effects that must be produced by speech.
Its subdivisions are proof and refutation, the arousing of emotions (such as pity, fear, anger, and the like), and also amplification and belittlement.
Clearly one must draw on the same forms in the events as well, whenever it is necessary to make them appear pitiable, terrible, important, or probable;

there is only this much difference, that the events must appear so without verbal instruction, whereas the effects in speech must be produced by the speaker and arise from his words. For what would be the speaker's task if the desired impression were already evident without speech?

As for diction, one branch of inquiry concerns the modes of utterance, knowledge of which belongs to the art of delivery and to the master of that craft—for instance, what is a command, a prayer, a narrative, a threat, a question, an answer, and anything else of the sort.

For no criticism worth taking seriously can be brought against the art of poetry based on knowledge or ignorance of these matters. Who would suppose that there is a fault in what Protagoras censures—that Homer, intending to pray, issues a command when he says
Sing, goddess, of the wrath? For telling someone to do or not to do something, he says, is a command.
Let us therefore pass over this as an inquiry belonging to another art and not to poetics.
The parts of all diction are these: letter, syllable, conjunction, noun, verb, joint-word, inflection, and utterance.
A letter is an indivisible sound—not just any sound, however, but one from which an intelligible sound can naturally arise; for animals too make indivisible sounds, none of which I call a letter.

The subdivisions of this are the vowel, the semivowel, and the mute. A vowel is a letter having an audible sound without contact of the vocal organs; a semivowel is one having an audible sound with contact, such as S and R; a mute is one with contact that has no sound of its own, yet becomes audible when combined with letters that have some sound, such as G and D.

These differ according to the configurations of the mouth and the places of articulation, aspiration and unaspiration, length and shortness, and also acute, grave, and intermediate pitch; it belongs to metrics to examine each of these in detail.

A syllable is a non-significant sound composed of a mute and a letter that has sound: for GR without A is a syllable, and so is it with A, as GRA. Yet examining the differences of these too belongs to metrics.

A conjunction is a non-significant sound which neither hinders nor produces a single significant sound out of several sounds, naturally placed either at the ends or in the middle, which it is not proper to place at the beginning of a sentence by itself—such as men, etoi, de; or a non-significant sound which out of several sounds—each significant—naturally produces a single significant sound.

A joint-word is a non-significant sound that marks the beginning, end, or division of an utterance, such as amphi, peri, and the rest; or a non-significant sound which neither hinders nor produces a single significant sound out of several sounds, naturally placed both at the ends and in the middle.

A noun is a composite significant sound without tense, no part of which is significant by itself; for in compound nouns we do not use the parts as significant by themselves—for example, in "Theodorus" the part "-dorus" has no meaning.

A verb is a composite significant sound with tense, no part of which is significant by itself, just as with nouns: for "man" or "white" does not indicate when, whereas "walks" or "has walked" additionally indicates present time in the one case and past time in the other.

Inflection of a noun or verb is that which indicates "of this" or "to this" and the like; or singular and plural, such as "men" or "man"; or modes of delivery, such as question or command—for "Did he walk?" or "Walk!" is an inflection of the verb in these modes.
An utterance is a composite significant sound, some parts of which signify something by themselves

(for not every utterance consists of verbs and nouns—for example, the definition of "man"—but it is possible to have an utterance without verbs; it will, however, always have some significant part), such as "Cleon" in "Cleon walks."

An utterance is one in two ways: either as signifying one thing, or as linking several things by a conjunction; thus the Iliad is one by conjunction, whereas the definition of "man" is one by signifying one thing.
Of nouns, one kind is simple—by simple I mean one not composed of significant parts, such as "earth"—and the other is compound.
Of the latter, one kind is composed of a significant and a non-significant part (though not significant and non-significant within the noun itself), and the other of two significant parts.
There could also be a triple, quadruple, or multiple noun, such as most of the names used by the Massaliots, "Hermocaicoxanthus" . . .
Every noun is either a standard word, a loanword, a metaphor, an ornament, a coined word, a lengthened word, a shortened word, or an altered word.
By "standard word" I mean one used by each community itself,

and by "loanword" one used by other communities. Clearly, then, the same word can be both a loanword and a standard word, though not to the same people: for "sigynon" (spear) is a standard word to Cyprians, but a loanword to us.
Metaphor is the application of a word belonging to something else, either from genus to species, or from species to genus, or from species to species, or by analogy.
By "from genus to species" I mean, for example, Here stands my ship, for lying at anchor is a species of standing.
From species to genus: Truly ten thousand noble deeds has Odysseus wrought, for "ten thousand" is a great number, which the poet here uses instead of "many."

From species to species: drawing off the life with bronze and cutting with unyielding bronze; here the poet has used "drawing off" for "cutting" and "cutting" for "drawing off," since both are forms of taking away.
By "analogy" I mean when the second term stands to the first as the fourth stands to the third; for then the poet will say the fourth instead of the second, or the second instead of the fourth.

And sometimes they add the term to which the replaced word is related. For example, a wine-cup stands to Dionysus as a shield stands to Ares; so the poet will call the wine-cup "the shield of Dionysus" and the shield "the wine-cup of Ares."
Or as old age is to life, so evening is to day; so one will call evening "the old age of day," or, as Empedocles does, call old age "the evening of life" or "the sunset of life."

In some cases there is no established name for one of the analogous terms, yet it will still be expressed in the same way: for example, scattering seed is called "sowing," whereas scattering flame from the sun has no name; yet this stands to the sun as sowing stands to seed, and therefore it has been said, sowing the god-created flame.
One can also use this mode of metaphor in another way: by applying the borrowed term and denying one of its proper attributes,
for instance, calling the shield not "the wine-cup of Ares," but "the wineless cup" . . .
A coined word is one not used by anyone at all, which the poet invents himself; some words appear to be of this kind, such as "sprouters" (ernyges) for horns and "prayer" (areter) for priest.
A word is lengthened or shortened: lengthened if it uses a longer vowel than its proper one or has an extra syllable inserted; shortened if something has been removed from it.
Examples of lengthening are "poleeos" for "poleos" and "Peleiadeo" for "Peleidou"; examples of shortening are "kri" (barley), "do" (house), and one eye (ops) is shared by both.
An altered word is when the poet leaves part of the usual word and invents the rest, as on the right-hand (dexiteron) breast instead of "right" (dexion).
Of nouns themselves, some are masculine, some feminine, and some neuter.
Masculine are all that end in N, R, and S, and all letters compounded with S (of which there are two, Ps and X); feminine are all that end in the vowels that are always long,
namely long E and long O, and among the lengthenable vowels, A.
Thus the number of endings for masculine and feminine nouns turns out to be equal, since Ps and X are compounds.
No noun ends in a mute, nor in a short vowel.
Only three end in I: meli (honey), kommi (gum), and peperi (pepper); five end in U. Neuter nouns end in these vowels, and in N and S.
The excellence of diction is to be clear and not mean.
Now the clearest diction is that composed of standard words, but it is mean; examples are the poetry of Cleophon and that of Sthenelus.
Dignified and elevated above the ordinary is diction that uses unfamiliar words; by "unfamiliar" I mean loanwords, metaphors, lengthenings, and everything departing from standard usage.
Yet if someone composes entirely in such words, it will be either a riddle or barbarism: if of metaphors, a riddle; if of loanwords, barbarism.

For the very nature of a riddle is to express actual facts while combining impossibilities. Now this cannot be done by combining ordinary words, but with metaphors it is possible—for example, I saw a man gluing bronze upon a man with fire, and the like.
A composition of loanwords is barbarism.

Therefore one needs a certain blend of these elements: the one kind—loanwords, metaphors, ornaments, and the other species mentioned—will keep the diction from being ordinary and mean, while standard words will provide clarity.

No small contribution to clarity and elevation of diction is made by lengthenings, shortenings, and alterations of words: by differing from the standard form and departing from custom, they will prevent the diction from being ordinary, while by retaining a share of what is customary, clarity will be preserved.

Therefore those who censure this manner of language and ridicule the poet—like the elder Euclides, claiming it is easy to compose poetry if one is allowed to lengthen syllables as much as one pleases, and parodying it in the very wording: I saw Epichares walking to Marathon, and not having desired his hellebore—are wrong to find fault.
To be visibly using this device to excess is indeed laughable, but moderation is a requirement common to all parts of diction;
for someone who used metaphors, loanwords, and the other forms inappropriately and deliberately for comic effect would produce the same result.
How much difference appropriateness makes may be observed in epic verse by substituting ordinary words into the meter.

And in the case of loanwords, metaphors, and the other forms, by substituting standard words one can see that what we say is true. For instance, Aeschylus and Euripides composed the same iambic line, with Euripides changing only a single word—putting a rare word in place of a familiar standard word—and the one line appears fine while the other appears cheap. For Aeschylus in his Philoctetes wrote,
The ulcer that eats the flesh of my foot, whereas Euripides substituted "feasts upon" for "eats." Or take
And now a puny, worthless, unseemly man, if one were to say, substituting standard words,
And now a small, weak, ugly man; or
Setting down an unseemly stool and a puny table,
Setting down a shabby stool and a small table; or the shores resound, compared with "the shores shout."

Again, Ariphrades used to ridicule the tragic poets because they use expressions that no one would use in ordinary conversation, such as "domaton apo" instead of "apo domaton" (from the house), "sethen" (of thee), "ego de nin" (and I him), "Achilleos peri" instead of "peri Achilleos" (concerning Achilles), and all other such phrases.
Precisely because they are not part of standard usage, all such expressions elevate the diction above the ordinary; and that is what Ariphrades failed to understand.
It is a great thing to use each of the forms mentioned appropriately, including compound words and loanwords, but by far the greatest thing is to be a master of metaphor.
For this alone cannot be acquired from another person and is a mark of natural genius; since to make good metaphors is to perceive likeness.
Of words, compounds are best suited to dithyrambs, loanwords to heroic verse, and metaphors to iambics.

In heroic verse all the forms mentioned are useful; in iambics, because they imitate ordinary speech as closely as possible, those words are fitting which one might also use in prose—namely, standard words, metaphors, and ornaments.
Let what we have said suffice, then, regarding tragedy and imitation in action.

As for narrative imitation in verse, it is clear that its plots should be constructed dramatically, just as in tragedies, and around a single action that is whole and complete, having a beginning, middle, and end, so that like a single whole living creature it may produce its proper pleasure;

and its constructions must not resemble histories, in which one must necessarily set forth not a single action but a single period of time—everything that happened during that period to one person or to several, each event standing in merely casual relation to the others.

For just as at the very same time the sea-battle at Salamis and the battle against the Carthaginians in Sicily took place without converging toward the same end, so too in successive periods one thing sometimes happens after another without any single end resulting from them.
Yet nearly all the epic poets do just this.

Hence, as we have already said, in this respect too Homer would appear inspired compared with the rest, because he did not attempt to compose a poem about the whole war, even though it had a beginning and an end; for the plot would have been too large and not easily taken in at a single view, or if moderated in length, overly entangled in its variety. Instead, selecting a single part, he has used many of the other events as episodes—such as the Catalogue of Ships and other episodes with which he twice diversifies his poem.
The other poets, however, compose about a single person, a single period of time, and a single action of many parts—like the author of the Cypria and of the Little Iliad.

Consequently, from the Iliad and the Odyssey only one tragedy, or at most two, can be made from each, whereas many can be made from the Cypria, and from the Little Iliad more than eight, such as the Judgment of Arms, Philoctetes, Neoptolemus, Eurypylus, the Begging, the Laconian Women, the Sack of Troy, and the Departure and Sinon and the Trojan Women.
Furthermore, epic poetry must have the same species as tragedy—for it must be simple, complex, focused on character, or focused on suffering—
and the same constituent parts, apart from song-making and spectacle; for it needs reversals, recognitions, and sufferings, and also its thought and diction must be well crafted.

Homer was the first to use all of these, and he used them adequately. Indeed, each of his poems is constructed accordingly: the Iliad is simple and centered on suffering, while the Odyssey is complex (for it is recognition throughout) and centered on character; and in addition, in diction and thought he has surpassed all others.
Epic poetry differs from tragedy in the length of its structure and in its meter.

As for length, the limit already stated is sufficient: it must be possible to take in the beginning and the end in a single view. This would be achieved if the compositions were shorter than the ancient epics, and matched the length of the group of tragedies presented at a single sitting.

Epic poetry has a great special capacity for extending its magnitude, because in tragedy it is not possible to imitate many parts of the action happening simultaneously, but only the part on stage performed by the actors; whereas in epic, because it is narrative, one can represent many parts being carried out simultaneously, and provided these are germane, the poem's scope is enlarged.
Thus epic has this advantage for magnificence, for varying the listener's interest, and for enriching the poem with unlike episodes; for uniformity quickly satiates and causes tragedies to fail.
The heroic meter has proven fitting through experience. If someone were to compose a narrative imitation in any other meter, or in many meters, it would appear inappropriate;
for the heroic is the most stately and weightiest of meters (which is why it admits loanwords and metaphors most readily, since narrative imitation too stands out from the rest),
whereas the iambic and tetrameter are lively, the tetrameter suited to dancing and the iambic to action.
It would be even more absurd if someone mixed them, as Chaeremon did.
Therefore no one has composed a long work in any meter other than the heroic; rather, as we said, nature herself teaches poets to choose what is appropriate to it.
Homer deserves praise for many other things, and especially because he alone of the poets is not unaware of what he himself ought to do.

For the poet himself should say as little as possible, since it is not in speaking in his own person that he is an imitator. Now the other poets perform in their own person throughout, and imitate little and rarely; whereas Homer, after a brief prelude, straightaway brings on a man, a woman, or some other character, and none without character, but all possessing character.

One must indeed create a sense of wonder in tragedies, but epic admits the irrational to a greater degree—and it is through the irrational that wonder chiefly arises—because in epic we do not see the agent.

Thus the circumstances of the pursuit of Hector would appear ridiculous on stage—the Greeks standing still and not pursuing, and Achilles shaking his head at them—whereas in epic this passes unnoticed.
Wonder is pleasurable; a sign of this is that everyone exaggerates when telling a story, thinking to give pleasure.

Homer above all has also taught the other poets how to tell falsehoods properly. This is a matter of false inference. For people suppose that whenever B exists if A exists, or B happens if A happens, then if the consequent B exists, the antecedent A also exists or happens; yet this is a fallacy. Therefore, if the first thing is false, but something else must necessarily exist or happen if it is true, the poet should add that consequent; for because our mind knows the consequent to be true, it falsely infers that the antecedent is true as well. An example of this is the passage from the Washing Scene.
One should prefer plausible impossibilities to unconvincing possibilities.

Plots should not be constructed out of irrational parts; ideally they should contain nothing irrational at all, or else it should lie outside the story—like Oedipus' not knowing how Laius died—and not inside the drama, like the messengers reporting the Pythian Games in the Electra, or the man in the Mysians who travels all the way from Tegea to Mysia without speaking.

To say that otherwise the plot would have been ruined is ridiculous: one should not construct such plots in the first place. But if the poet does admit an irrationality and it appears to be handled more reasonably, even an absurdity may be accepted;

for even the irrationalities in the Odyssey concerning Odysseus' being put ashore would clearly be intolerable if a bad poet had composed them; as it is, the poet conceals the absurdity by sweetening it with his other excellences.
Diction should be elaborated in the inactive parts, which display neither character nor thought; for overly brilliant diction, on the other hand, obscures both character and thought.
Regarding critical problems and their solutions, how many species they have and what they are will become clear if we examine them as follows.

Since the poet is an imitator, just like a painter or any other maker of images, he must always imitate one of three things: either things as they were or are, or things as people say and think they are, or things as they ought to be.
These are expressed in diction that includes loanwords, metaphors, and many modifications of language;
for we grant these to poets. Furthermore, the standard of correctness is not the same in politics and in poetry, nor in any other art and in poetry.
Within the art of poetry itself, error is of two kinds: essential and incidental.

If the poet chose to imitate something and failed through lack of ability, the error is essential to the art; but if he made an incorrect choice—for example, portraying a horse with both right legs thrown forward at once—or committed an error pertaining to a particular art, such as medicine or any other art or impossibilities have been composed whatsoever, the error is not essential to poetry.

Accordingly, one must resolve the criticisms in critical problems by examining them from these standpoints. First, criticisms concerning the art itself: if impossibilities have been composed, that is an error;
yet it is right if it achieves the end of the art itself (and its end has been stated)—if in this way it makes either that part or another part more astonishing. An example is the pursuit of Hector.

If, however, the end could have been achieved better or no less well while observing the art dealing with those matters, to have erred it is not right; for if possible there should be no error at all.

Again, to which category does the error belong—those essential to the art, or something incidental? For it is a lesser fault not to know that a female deer has no horns than to paint one unconvincingly.

In addition, if a poem is criticized for not being true, perhaps it represents things as they ought to be—just as Sophocles said that he portrayed people as they ought to be, while Euripides portrayed them as they are; this is how the objection should be resolved.
If it is neither, one may answer that this is what people say, as in stories about the gods:
perhaps it is neither better to speak so nor true, and it may happen to be as Xenophanes says; still, that is what people say.

Other things are perhaps not better, yet that is how they were, such as the passage about the weapons, and their spears stood upright on their butt-spikes; for that was the custom then, just as it still is among the Illyrians.

As to whether something has been said or done well or badly by a character, one must examine not only the deed or word itself to see whether it is admirable or base, but also the person who does or says it, to whom, when, by what means, and for what end—for instance, whether it is to achieve a greater good or to avert a greater evil.

Other objections must be resolved by looking to the diction—for example, by recognizing a loanword in first the mules (oureas), for perhaps he means not mules, but sentries; and of Dolon, who indeed was ill in form (eidos), not ill-proportioned in body, but ugly in face, since Cretans use "well-formed" (eueides) to mean "handsome-faced"; and mix it livelier (zoroteron), not "unmixed" as for drunkards, but "more quickly."

Another expression is used metaphorically, such as all gods and men slept all night long, while at the same time he says, whenever he gazed on the Trojan plain, the din of flutes and pipes; for "all" is used instead of "many" by metaphor, since "all" is a kind of "many." So too alone has no share is metaphorical, for the best-known is called "alone."
Other difficulties are resolved by accentuation, as Hippias of Thasos resolved we grant (didomen) him to win glory and part of which (ou) rots in the rain.
Others by punctuation, as in Empedocles: Straightaway things grew mortal that before had learned to be immortal, and things formerly pure were mixed.
Others by ambiguity, as more (pleo) of the night has passed, for "pleio" is ambiguous.

Others by linguistic custom: people call mixed wine "wine," whence is coined a greave of newly wrought tin, and they call ironworkers "coppersmiths," whence Ganymede is said to pour wine for Zeus, though the gods do not drink wine. This last, however, could also be explained by metaphor.

Whenever a word seems to signify some contradiction, one must consider how many meanings it can bear in the passage—for instance, in there the bronze spear was checked, in how many ways "being checked there" can be taken,
in this sense or in that, according to how one might best understand it—the opposite of what

Glaucon describes, when he says that some critics make an unreasonable assumption beforehand, pass judgment on that basis, and then reason from it, censuring the poet as if he had said whatever they think, if it contradicts their own notion.

This is what has happened in the case of Icarius: they assume he was a Laconian, and therefore find it absurd that Telemachus did not meet him when he went to Lacedaemon. Yet perhaps the truth is as the Cephallenians say: they claim that Odysseus married from among them and that the father was Icadius, not Icarius; so the problem is probably due to a mistake.
In general, the impossible must be referred to the requirements of poetry, or to what is better, or to received opinion.
For the purposes of poetry, a convincing impossibility is preferable to an unconvincing possibility;
. . . that people should be such as Zeuxis painted them, yes, for the better; since the ideal model should surpass reality.
Irrationalities should be referred to what people say, and also to the fact that at times a thing is not irrational, since it is probable that things should happen even contrary to probability.

Apparent contradictions in speech should be examined just like refutations in dialectic—whether the same thing is meant, in relation to the same thing, and in the same way—so that we judge the poet either by what he himself says or by what an intelligent person would assume.

Censure of irrationality and of depravity is justified when, without any necessity, the poet makes no real use of the irrationality—as Euripides does with Aegeus—or of the wickedness, as in the Orestes with that of Menelaus.

Thus criticisms are brought under five heads: as impossible, irrational, harmful, contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness. The solutions must be sought from the headings stated above, which are twelve in number.
One might raise the question whether epic imitation or tragic imitation is better.
If the less vulgar is better, and such is always that addressed to better spectators, it is very clear that the art which imitates everything is vulgar.

For supposing the audience will not perceive unless the performer adds it himself, they make excessive movements—like bad flute-players whirling around if they have to imitate a discus, or dragging at the chorus-leader when playing the Scylla.

Tragedy, then, is said to be like this, just as the older actors viewed those who came after them: Mynniscus called Callippides an ape for overacting so wildly, and the same opinion was held of Pindarus. And as these actors stand to the older ones, so the entire art of tragedy is said to stand to epic.
They say, then, that epic is addressed to refined spectators who have no need of gestures, whereas tragedy is addressed to inferior ones; if, then, it is vulgar, it would clearly be inferior.

In the first place, this accusation applies not to the art of poetry, but to the art of acting, since it is also possible to overdo gestures while reciting epic—as Sosistratus does did—and while singing in competition, as Mnasitheus of Opus used to do.

Secondly, not all movement is to be rejected—any more than dancing is—but only that of inferior people, which is precisely what was criticized in Callippides and nowadays in others, for imitating women who are not freeborn.

Further, tragedy achieves its proper effect even without movement, just like epic; for through reading alone its quality is manifest. If, therefore, it is superior in other respects, this feature at least does not necessarily belong to it.
Next, because tragedy possesses everything that epic possesses
(for it may even use the epic meter), and in addition has no small part in music and spectacle, through which its pleasures are constituted most vividly;
and further, it possesses vividness both in reading and in performance.

Moreover, the end of its imitation is achieved in a shorter compass (for what is more concentrated is more pleasurable than what is diluted over a long stretch of time—for instance, if someone were to put Sophocles' Oedipus into as many lines as the Iliad).

Again, the imitation of epic poets has less unity (a sign of this is that out of any single epic imitation several tragedies are made), so that if they compose a single plot, either it is presented briefly and appears curtailed, or it follows the length of the meter and appears watery; by this I mean if it is composed of several actions,

just as the Iliad and the Odyssey have many such parts which even by themselves possess magnitude—and yet those poems are constructed as well as possible and are as nearly as possible an imitation of a single action.

If, then, tragedy excels in all these respects, and also in achieving the proper function of the art (for they must produce not just any chance pleasure, but the one already stated), it is clear that tragedy would be superior, since it attains its end more fully than epic.

Regarding tragedy and epic, then—both themselves and their species and parts, how many they are and how they differ, what are the causes of success or failure, and regarding critical problems and their solutions—let this much suffice. . . .
